about: The scripted AI lesson for p1-power (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p1-energy-stores and p1-efficiency.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about power: how fast energy is transferred, how to work it out, and the units it is measured in.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. What unit is energy measured in?
steps.right: Yes: energy is measured in joules (J).

wrong.newton: Not quite: joules (J). Newtons are the unit of force.
wrong.metre: Not quite: joules (J). Metres measure distance.

idk.hint: The unit of energy is named after the scientist James Joule. Which button is it?

steps.question: Second: you lift a box onto a high shelf. Which store of the box fills up?
steps.right: Yes: raising the box fills its gravitational potential store.

wrong.other: Not quite: gravitational potential, the store for raised things.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: once it is on the shelf the box is still. Raising it fills its gravitational potential store.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: nothing is stretched. Raising the box fills its gravitational potential store.

idk.hint: The box ends up higher. Which store is for raised things?

steps.answerWhy: Raising the box fills its gravitational potential store.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Two kettles each heat the same water by the same amount. One takes 2 minutes and the other takes 4. Both transfer the same energy to the water, but the first does it twice as fast.
A rate is how much happens in a given time, such as each second. Speed is a rate: the metres you travel each second.
The rate at which energy is transferred is called power: the energy transferred each second. The faster kettle has twice the power.
Power is measured in watts (W). 1 watt is 1 joule transferred every second.

steps.question: A lamp transfers 60 J every second. What is its power?

wrong.unit: Nearly: the number is right, but power is in watts, so 60 W.
wrong.one: Not quite: 60 W. 1 W would be just 1 J in each second.

idk.hint: Count the joules transferred in one second. That number is the power in watts.

steps.answerWhy: 60 J in each second is a power of 60 W.

steps.text: The equation is P = E ÷ t: power = energy transferred ÷ time. P is the power in watts (W), E is the energy transferred in joules (J) and t is the time in seconds (s).

A more powerful machine does not always transfer more energy in total: it transfers energy faster. Lifting a car to the same height takes the same energy whether a crane takes 20 s or 5 s. The faster crane takes a quarter of the time, so it has four times the power.

steps.question: Two motors lift the same load to the same height. Motor X takes 10 s and motor Y takes 30 s. Which is true?

options.text: X has three times the power of Y
X transfers more energy than Y
Y has more power, because it works for longer

steps.right: Yes: they transfer the same energy, but X does it in a third of the time, so X has three times the power.

wrong.other: Not quite. X has three times the power: the same energy in a third of the time.
wrong.energy: Not quite: lifting the same load to the same height takes the same energy. X transfers it in a third of the time, so X has three times the power.
wrong.longer: Not quite: taking longer means a lower power. X transfers the same energy in a third of the time, so X has three times the power.

idk.hint: Both transfer the same energy. Which motor transfers it faster, and how many times faster?

steps.answerWhy: The energy is the same, but X transfers it in a third of the time, so X has three times the power.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is power, and what unit is it measured in?
points: the energy transferred each second (the rate of energy transfer)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: power is the energy transferred each second, measured in watts.

steps.text: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A light bulb transfers 100 J in 10 s. What is its power?
steps: Write the equation: P = E ÷ t.

steps.question: Your turn. A runner transfers 12 000 J in 60 s. What is the runner's power, in watts?

wrong.times: Not quite: 200 W. Divide the energy by the time, do not multiply: 12 000 ÷ 60 = 200 W.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 200 W. Divide the energy by the time: P = 12 000 ÷ 60 = 200 W.

idk.hint: Use P = E ÷ t: divide the energy, 12 000, by the time, 60.

steps.text: Big powers are often given in kilowatts (kW): 1 kW = 1000 W. A 2 kW heater has a power of 2000 W.
The power output of a power station is given in megawatts (MW): 1 MW = 1 000 000 W, a million watts.
Before you calculate, change kilowatts and megawatts into watts, and minutes into seconds: 1 minute is 60 s.
To find the energy or the time, put the numbers into P = E ÷ t first, then rearrange.
Here is a worked example of finding the energy. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: A 50 W lamp is on for 20 s. How much energy does it transfer?
steps: Put the numbers into P = E ÷ t: 50 = E ÷ 20.

steps.text: And here is a worked example of finding the time. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: How long does a 2000 W heater take to transfer 36 000 J?
steps: Put the numbers into P = E ÷ t: 2000 = 36 000 ÷ t.
Multiply both sides by t: 2000 × t = 36 000.
Divide both sides by 2000: t = 36 000 ÷ 2000 = 18 s.

steps.question: A 3 kW oven is on for 20 s. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?

wrong.nokw: Not quite: 60 000 J. Change kilowatts to watts first: 3 kW = 3000 W. Then E = 3000 × 20 = 60 000 J.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 60 000 J. To find the energy, multiply: E = P × t = 3000 × 20 = 60 000 J.

idk.hint: First, 3 kW in watts is 3000 W. Then multiply by the time, 20 s.

steps.question: How long does a 500 W microwave take to transfer 30 000 J, in seconds?

wrong.times: Not quite: 60 s. To find the time, divide the energy by the power: 30 000 ÷ 500 = 60 s.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 60 s. Divide the energy by the power: t = 30 000 ÷ 500 = 60 s.

idk.hint: Use t = E ÷ P: divide 30 000 by 500.

steps.question: A 2.5 kW kettle is on for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?

wrong.none: Not quite: 300 000 J. Both need changing: 2.5 kW = 2500 W, and 2 minutes = 120 s. Then E = 2500 × 120 = 300 000 J.
wrong.nokw: Not quite: 300 000 J. The time is right in seconds, but the power must be in watts: 2.5 kW = 2500 W. E = 2500 × 120 = 300 000 J.
wrong.nomin: Not quite: 300 000 J. The power is right in watts, but the time must be in seconds: 2 minutes = 120 s. E = 2500 × 120 = 300 000 J.

idk.hint: Change both: 2.5 kW is 2500 W, and 2 minutes is 120 s. Then multiply them.

steps.prompt: In one line: what units must the power, energy and time be in before you use P = E ÷ t?
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: power in watts, energy in joules and time in seconds.

steps.text: Some real powers: a hairdryer is about 2000 W, a kettle 2000 to 3000 W, and an electric car's motor 100 to 300 kW.
A large power station gives out about 1 to 2 gigawatts (GW). A gigawatt is 1000 MW, or 1 000 000 000 W.

steps.question: Which of these transfers energy fastest: a 0.5 MW wind turbine, a 3000 W kettle or a 300 kW car motor?
steps.right: Yes: 0.5 MW is 500 000 W, the car motor is 300 000 W and the kettle 3000 W.

wrong.other: Not quite: the wind turbine. 0.5 MW is 500 000 W, more than 300 000 W or 3000 W.
wrong.car: Not quite: 300 kW is 300 000 W, but 0.5 MW is 500 000 W, so the turbine transfers energy faster.
wrong.kettle: Not quite: 3000 is the biggest number, but the units differ. In watts: kettle 3000 W, car motor 300 000 W, turbine 500 000 W.

idk.hint: Change each into watts: 1 MW = 1 000 000 W and 1 kW = 1000 W. Then compare.

steps.answerWhy: In watts: the turbine is 500 000 W, the car motor 300 000 W and the kettle 3000 W, so the turbine is fastest.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does it mean that a kettle has a higher power than a phone charger?
points: the kettle transfers more energy each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the kettle transfers more energy each second than the charger.

steps.text: When a force moves an object, it transfers energy. The energy transferred when a force moves something is called the work done.
The equation is W = F × s: work done = force × distance. W is the work done in joules (J), F is the force in newtons (N) and s is the distance moved in the direction of the force, in metres (m).
Careful: in this equation W stands for work done and s for distance, not watts and seconds.
One joule of work is done when a force of 1 newton moves something 1 metre. A newton-metre (N m) is therefore the same as a joule: 20 N m is 20 J.
Here is a worked example. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: A force of 3000 N pushes a car 20 m. How much work is done?
steps: Write the equation: W = F × s.

steps.question: Your turn. A force of 50 N pushes a box 4 m along the floor. How much work is done, in joules?

wrong.other: Not quite: 200 J. W = F × s = 50 × 4 = 200 J.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 200 J. Multiply the force by the distance: 50 × 4 = 200 J.
wrong.add: Not quite: 200 J. Multiply, do not add: 50 × 4 = 200 J.

idk.hint: Use W = F s: multiply the force, 50, by the distance, 4.

steps.text: You met this at the start: lifting a box gives it energy in its gravitational potential store. That energy comes from the work done by the lifting force.
Pushing a box along a rough floor against friction makes the box and the floor warmer, so energy goes into their thermal stores.

steps.question: A box is pushed along a rough floor at a steady speed. Where does the work done go?

options.text: Into the thermal stores of the box and the floor
Into the box's gravitational potential store

steps.right: Yes: pushing against friction warms the box and the floor, so the work done goes into their thermal stores.

wrong.other: Not quite: into the thermal stores of the box and the floor, because friction warms them.
wrong.gpe: Not quite: the box stays at the same height, so its gravitational potential store does not change. Friction warms the box and floor.
wrong.chem: Not quite: nothing burns or reacts. Friction warms the box and the floor, so the energy goes into their thermal stores.

idk.hint: The box is not raised or speeded up, but rubbing on the floor warms things. Which store is about warmth?

steps.answerWhy: Pushing against friction warms the box and the floor, so the work done goes into their thermal stores.

steps.text: Power is also the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t. P is the power, in watts; W is the work done, in joules; t is the time, in seconds.

steps.question: A crane does 60 000 J of work lifting a load in 30 s. What is its power, in watts?
steps.right: Yes: 2000 W. Power = work done ÷ time = 60 000 J ÷ 30 s = 2000 W.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2000 W. Power = work done ÷ time = 60 000 J ÷ 30 s = 2000 W.
wrong.times: Not quite: 2000 W. Divide the work done by the time: 60 000 J ÷ 30 s = 2000 W.

idk.hint: Use P = W ÷ t: divide 60 000 by 30.

steps.answerWhy: Power = work done ÷ time = 60 000 J ÷ 30 s = 2000 W.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is work done?
points: the energy transferred when a force moves something
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: work done is the energy transferred when a force moves something.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a motor transfers 500 J in 10 s. What is its power, in watts?

wrong.other: Not quite: 50 W. P = E ÷ t = 500 ÷ 10 = 50 W.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a heater has a power of 3 kW. What is that in watts?

wrong.other: Not quite: 3000 W. 1 kW = 1000 W, so 3 kW = 3000 W.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a 100 W lamp is on for 1 minute. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?
steps.right: Yes: 1 minute is 60 s, and E = P × t = 100 × 60 = 6000 J.

wrong.other: Not quite: 6000 J. 1 minute is 60 s, and E = P × t = 100 × 60 = 6000 J.

steps.answerWhy: 1 minute is 60 s, so E = P × t = 100 × 60 = 6000 J.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: what unit is power measured in?
steps.right: Yes: watts. 1 W is 1 J each second.

wrong.other: Not quite: watts. 1 W is 1 J each second.
wrong.w1: Not quite: joules measure energy. Power, the energy each second, is measured in watts.
wrong.w2: Not quite: newtons measure force. Power is measured in watts.

steps.answerWhy: Power is measured in watts: 1 W is 1 J each second.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: a force of 20 N moves a box 5 m. How much work is done, in joules?

wrong.other: Not quite: 100 J. W = F × s = 20 × 5 = 100 J.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: a 2 kW heater warms a room in 30 minutes. How long would a 1 kW heater take to transfer the same energy?
steps.right: Yes: half the power, so twice the time for the same energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: 60 minutes. Half the power transfers the same energy in twice the time.
wrong.w1: Not quite: 60 minutes. Less power means slower, so it takes longer, not shorter: half the power, twice the time.
wrong.w2: Not quite: 60 minutes. The power does matter: half the power transfers the same energy in twice the time.

steps.answerWhy: Half the power transfers the same energy in twice the time: 60 minutes.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
